bio.en: Roger Martin is one of the world's most trusted strategy advisors, professor emeritus at the Rotman School of Management at the University of Toronto, and author of the classic Playing to Win.
bio.zh: Roger Martin 是全球最受信赖的战略顾问之一，多伦多大学罗特曼管理学院荣休教授，也是经典著作《赢得胜利》（Playing to Win）的作者。

summary.en: Roger argues that strategy is an integrative activity answering five questions - winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, required capabilities, and management systems - and that you must choose either differentiation or low cost. He critiques how business schools teach strategy poorly, and insists great strategists are made through practice, not born. The episode gives ground-level PMs and ICs a practical framework for crafting real strategy.
summary.zh: Roger 主张战略是一项“整合性”活动，需回答五个问题——制胜抱负、在何处竞争、如何取胜、所需能力、以及支撑性管理体系——并且必须在“差异化”与“低成本”之间二选一。他批评商学院对战略的教学方式之多谬，并坚称伟大的战略家是练出来的，而非天生的。本期为一线 PM 与独立贡献者提供了一套制定真正战略的实用框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why are so many people bad at strategy?
turns.zh: 为什么这么多人不擅长战略？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: What's taught now in business schools generally sucks. People aren't prepared educationally, and they sure don't get prepared for it in companies. It's intellectually challenging and it's emotionally intimidating.
turns.zh: 如今商学院里教授的内容普遍很糟糕。学生们在教育方面准备不足，企业里更是缺乏相关培训。这既需要智力挑战，又充满情感压迫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have something you call the strategy choice cascade.
turns.zh: 你提到的战略选择层级。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: You have to have answers to five questions. What's your winning aspiration? Where to play? How can you win? What capabilities do you have to have that your competitors don't? And then, what enabling management systems do you have to put in place? For the most part, in the leading business schools, it's illegal to teach that.
turns.zh: 要回答五个问题：你的制胜愿景是什么？在哪里竞争？如何取胜？你拥有哪些竞争对手没有的能力？然后，你需要建立哪些赋能型管理体系？在顶尖商学院里，这些内容通常都是被禁止教授的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Playing to win, you talked about, and there's kind of these two routes.
turns.zh: 你提到的以赢为目标，基本上有两条路径。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: You have to be either differentiated or low cost, there's no way to protect yourself if you're not one of those two.
turns.zh: 要么差异化，要么低成本，如果不符合这两个条件，就无法保护自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you wanted to just leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 你还有什么想留给听众的启示吗？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: I have never met this mythical beast called a great natural strategist. Great strategists have all one thing in common, they just practice.
turns.zh: 我从未见过传说中的天生战略家这种神话般的存在。伟大的战略家都有一个共同点——他们不断实践。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just want to ask this broad question about strategy, why is strategy so hard? Why are so many people bad at strategy?
turns.zh: 我只想问一个关于战略的宽泛问题：为什么战略如此困难？为什么这么多人不擅长战略？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Perhaps the thing that makes it intellectually hardest is that it is an integrative activity. It answers to a bunch of questions that have to fit together and reinforce one another. So, that just makes it a little more complicated, it's not like saying, Lenny, what do you want for lunch? It's saying, Lenny, what kind of diet do you want that'll keep you healthy? And that includes breakfast, lunch, dinners, snacks, a whole bunch of other things that you got to fit together. So, it makes that harder to do intellectually. Another aspect of it is, it is intimidating. Strategy involves making choices to do some things and not other things, and it is often intimidating to say, oh dear, I have to cut these things off, and not do them, and actually make a decision that I'll be held accountable for potentially, or I'll even hold myself accountable for. (00:08:21): So, that's a second thing. It's harder emotionally, not harder intellectually. And then, there's the training aspect of it, the knowledge aspect of it, which is, what's taught now in strategy in business schools generally sucks. It's gone on a crazy theoretical bend, the strategy academy as a whole has fallen in love with a theory called the resource-based theory of the firm, that silly and nobody uses it out in the world. And so, students are no longer trained on useful strategy. And the other feeder into people learning strategy were the strategy consulting firms, but the strategy consulting firms, the so-called strategy consulting firms, do almost no strategy anymore because it's a little business compared to post-merger integration, digital transformation, and a bunch of other things. So, people aren't prepared educationally for it, and if they're not prepared educationally for it, then they sure don't get prepared for it in companies. It's intellectually challenging and it's emotionally intimidating.
turns.zh:
或许最具智力挑战性的一点在于，这是一项综合性活动。它需要解答一系列必须相互契合、相互印证的问题。因此，这就变得稍显复杂——这不像是问“莱尼，你午餐想吃什么？”，更像是问“莱尼，你想要怎样的饮食方案才能保持健康？”这涵盖了早餐、午餐、晚餐、零食等诸多环节，所有这些都需要统筹兼顾。因此，从智力层面而言，这确实更具挑战性。

另一个方面是，策略制定本身就令人却步。策略需要做出取舍——决定做某些事而非其他事。当你不得不说“哎呀，我得砍掉这些项目，不再做这些事”时，往往会感到心理压力。这种决定可能需要你为之负责，甚至要自我约束。（00:08:21）这就是第二个挑战——情感层面的困难，而非智力层面的。

再者，还有培训层面和知识层面的不足。当前商学院的战略教学普遍存在缺陷。理论研究已走向极端，整个战略学界痴迷于“基于资源的企业理论”这种过时且无人问津的理论。学生们已不再接受实用的战略思维训练。曾经为人们提供战略学习的渠道是战略咨询公司，但如今这些所谓的战略咨询公司几乎不再从事战略业务，因为相较于并购整合、数字化转型等热门领域，战略咨询已沦为小众业务。因此，人们在教育层面缺乏战略思维的准备，而若缺乏教育基础，企业层面的培养就更是难上加难。战略既具智力挑战，又充满情感压力，两者交织成重重阻碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On this point, you made about how schools are teaching strategy wrong, how do you describe what the wrong approach is?
turns.zh: 关于你提到的学校错误的战略教学方式，您能否具体说明错误的教学方法是什么？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: It's a theory that's sort of taken over, called the resource-based view of the firm, that was... In the world of academics, there's a weird place where the number one emotion is jealousy, and people were massively jealous of Mike Porter, who created many of the most important concepts of strategy when he wrote a book, Competitive Strategy, in 1980. And so, they needed to counter him because they just didn't like the fact that he was so prominent, and they decided they would say he was about positioning. So, they called his the positioning school, and they caricatured what he said, which he never did, but they said he said it's all about finding a place that is structurally attractive, and then milking it for everything you can. (00:10:43): We at the resource-based view of the firm think that strategy is all about building resources. And if you build resources, it's almost like if you build it, they will come. And that's what you should pay attention to. Now, the problem is, any resource that may be useful somewhere is not necessarily useful elsewhere. So, it begs the question, how would you think through what resources to invest in building? What would be a way of doing that, investing here, versus here, versus here? It's silent on that because it's a dumb theory, and it doesn't have anything useful to say, in my view, about that. (00:11:33): And so, when the students go out and say to their company, I'm going to do a VRIO analysis, or a VRIN, some people just roll their eyes at them, and so it doesn't get used. I've only seen it used, I've been in consulting companies for 42 years, and I've seen it used once. And the trust, as is usually the case, is that it's both. And that's why the model I use for strategies says a lot about where you play is important, that's one of the key questions, and your capabilities are important, and you've got to link those things together. But that's, for the most part in the leading business schools, it's illegal to teach that.
turns.zh: 有一套理论近来风靡一时——被称为"资源基础观"（resource-based view of the firm）。但在学术界，有个奇怪的现象：最普遍的情绪竟是嫉妒。人们对迈克·波特（Mike Porter）心怀妒忌——他在1980年出版《竞争战略》（Competitive Strategy）一书时，开创了许多战略学的重要概念。于是，人们不得不反击，因为不甘心看到他如此显赫。于是，他们将他的理论归为“定位学派”（positioning school），并曲解了他的观点，声称他主张的都是如何找到结构性有利的位置，然后尽可能榨取其价值。（00:10:43）：我们支持资源基础观的人，认为战略的核心在于构建资源。只要构建了资源，仿佛自然而然就能吸引客户。这才是你应该关注的重点。问题是，某个资源在某个地方有用，不代表在其他地方也有用。所以关键在于：如何筛选出值得投入的资源？如何在不同位置之间进行取舍？这个问题在理论中被忽视了，因为这套理论太蠢了，在我看来，它对此毫无建树。（00:11:33）：当学生们对公司说：“我要做VRIO分析”或“VRIN分析”时，很多人对此嗤之以鼻，这种方法根本行不通。我在咨询公司工作42年，只见过一次有人用它。通常的共识是两者兼顾。这就是为什么我采用的战略模型强调：选对战场至关重要，这是关键问题之一；同时能力也很重要，两者必须相互关联。但在顶尖商学院，这种理论甚至被视为禁忌。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 被禁止教授你的方法。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yes. I couldn't teach my approach at my own business school.
turns.zh: 是的。我自己在商学院时也不能教授我的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 什么？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: But when I was dean, the most powerful person, the departments, or areas as we call it, like strategic management is an area, they have 100% control over what's taught in strategic management, in finance, et cetera. The dean may be the most powerful person in the school, and I happened to be a super successful dean, so if anything, I was a super powerful dean, and students would beg me, they'd say, "Roger, you have 20 years of experience, you're sort of a famous consultant in strategy, and you've got these theories, please teach a course in it." Nope. I did do extracurricular stuff, where I had practice of one Saturday a year, teaching everything I knew to anybody who wanted to show up. But for credit, I was not allowed. And if you try to get a job at any business... The only exception might be Harvard Business School, maybe. But if you took the 49 other top business schools in America, and if asked the question, do you swear allegiance to the resource-based view of the firm? If you don't answer an enthusiastic yes, you have no chance of being hired, zero.
turns.zh: 但我担任院长时，最有权势的人——部门，或者像我们称之为的“战略管理”这样的领域——对战略管理、金融等课程内容拥有完全控制权。院长可能是学校里最有权势的人，而我恰好是一位非常成功的院长，所以如果说有什么不同的话，我算是个超级强大的院长。学生们会求我：“罗杰，你有20年的经验，是战略领域的知名顾问，还有这些理论，请开设一门课程吧。” 不行。我确实做过校外活动，每年有一个周六，把我所知的一切教给所有想来的人。但获得学分是不被允许的。如果你想在任何商学院谋职……唯一例外可能是哈佛商学院。但如果看看美国其他49所顶尖商学院，如果被问到“你是否宣誓效忠资源基础观？”如果你不热情地回答“是”，你就毫无机会被录用，零机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. This academia drama, I had no idea.
turns.zh: 哇。这种学术界的闹剧，我之前完全不知道。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: A loyalty test.
turns.zh: 忠诚测试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is unreal. Makes me even more excited to dive into your world, and your ways of seeing things. Before we do that, just we've had a few other strategy people on the podcast, it might be helpful to frame where they fit in the spectrum that you're describing. So-
turns.zh: 这简直太不可思议了。这让我更加迫切地想深入了解你的世界，了解你看待事物的方式。不过在我们深入之前，我们在播客上邀请过几位战略领域的专家，或许先讲讲他们在你所描述的策略范畴中的位置会更有帮助。那么——

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Oh, okay. I may not know all of them, but you give me-
turns.zh: 哦，好的。我可能不了解他们所有人，但你可以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine you do. So, we've had a Hamilton Helmer on the podcast, and then Richard Rumelt on the podcast. How do they relate, just for people to get into your stuff versus this dogma?
turns.zh: 我相信你了解的。我们邀请过汉密尔顿·赫尔默（Hamilton Helmer）和理查德·鲁梅尔特（Richard Rumelt）参加播客。他们之间的关系如何？对于那些想深入理解你的观点而非遵循教条的人来说，会有什么不同？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: So, one of them is an academic, and one of them is a quasi-academic, or non-academic, like me. I was a tenured professor for many years, but don't consider myself an academic guy. I don't think Hamilton does, though I've never asked him-
turns.zh: 其中一位是学者，一位是准学者，或者像我一样的非学者。我曾多年担任终身教授，但不认为自己是学者。不过汉密尔顿可能也不算学者，虽然我从未问过他——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's an investor now.
turns.zh: 他现在是投资者了。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: ... that question. Yeah. So, he's written a very, I think, useful book that would in some sense fit into my how to win box, right? I say strategies about how to win, and he has a, what I call, a categorical model. Here are categories of things that you should think about. If you're trying to win, here are seven ways of winning, and I categorize him as a non-academic practical strategy guy. Richard Rumelt is a now retired Tuck professor, and he is this hyper competition thing that he does. He also is of the, I'm jealous of Mike Porter kind of thing. So, I've got to say, Mike Porter is wrong, and here's how I am so right, and the competition doesn't take place in the way Mike says, where it's really stable, and whatever, it's really hyper competition, Mike Porter never in his entire life has said competition is stable, he's repeatedly said the opposite. (00:15:54): But in order to say I'm not like Mike Porter, and in fact, I distinguish myself by saying he's wrong, and I'm right, and so... I don't know. He seemed like a fine guy. I don't think that he, like most business academics, he doesn't know much about business. He hasn't gone out and practiced a lot. He came to our school, and gave a lecture because people loved hyper competition because he would blast Mike Porter, and he gave a example of Proctor and Gamble, I've been consulting at Proctor and Gamble, and know everything about Procter and Gamble, basically. (00:16:42): And what he said about Proctor and Gamble had zero to do with reality, like zero. It was just completely, utterly, absolutely wrong. And I asked him afterwards, just sort of like, "Why do you say that?" And he said, "Well, I think that's the way it worked." Are you kidding me? So, I'm not a fan of that piece of work. I would say it doesn't fit nicely into research-based view of the firm versus Mike Porter, it's sort of like, here's another lens to take on the world, and I'm going to take that lens, everything's hyper-competitive, and here's how you think about hyper-competition.
turns.zh: ……那个问题。是的。所以，他写了一本我认为非常有用的书，在某种程度上符合我的“如何取胜”的框架，对吧？我谈论的是如何取胜的策略，而他提出了一个我称之为分类模型的理论。这里有几个你应该思考的类别。如果你想赢，就有七种获胜方式。我把他归类为非学者的实用策略派。理查德·鲁梅尔特现在是塔克商学院的退休教授，他研究的是超级竞争。他还有那种“我嫉妒迈克·波特”的心态。所以我得说迈克·波特是错的，而我才是对的，竞争并非像迈克所说的那样稳定等等。（00:15:54）但为了表明我和迈克·波特不同，事实上我通过指出他的错误来彰显自己的正确性，所以……我不知道。他看起来是个不错的人。我不认为他像大多数商学院学者那样，对商业了解甚少。他没怎么实际操作过。他来我们学校做讲座时，人们热衷于超级竞争，因为他会抨击迈克·波特，还举了宝洁公司的例子。我曾在宝洁公司做过咨询，对宝洁公司了如指掌。（00:16:42）但他对宝洁公司的说法与现实毫无关联，完全错误。我事后问他：“你为什么这么说？”他说：“嗯，我认为就是这样运作的。”开什么玩笑？所以我不喜欢那本书。我得说它与基于研究的企业观不符，更像是另一种看待世界的视角，而我会选择这种视角——一切都是超级竞争，下面是如何思考超级竞争。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is fascinating. I love that we're spending some time on this, this is really helpful to hear the landscape of strategy minds. Okay, let's dive into your worldview, and maybe the simplest way is just, how do you define strategy? What is a strategy?
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。很高兴我们能花时间探讨这个话题，深入了解战略领域的不同观点真是太有帮助了。好吧，让我们深入你的世界观，也许最简单的方法就是，你如何定义战略？什么是战略？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Strategy is an integrated set of choices that compels desired customer action. So, the way I think about it is, there's a whole bunch of things a company controls, how many factories to build, how much R&D to do, in what areas, and how much advertising to do, how many people to hire, what to pay them, blah, blah, blah... Those are all the things under our control. What, Lenny, is the thing we have almost no control over? What, if we're a company?
turns.zh: 战略是一套整合的决策体系，旨在促使客户采取理想的行动。那么，我的理解是，企业能掌控诸多方面：建造多少工厂、投入多少研发资金、研发方向如何、投放多少广告、招聘多少员工、支付多少薪资等等……这些都是我们可控的因素。莱尼，企业几乎无法控制的关键因素是什么？如果我们是企业主，情况又如何？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What customers do.
turns.zh: 客户的行为。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah. We would like them to take some of these out of their pocket and give them to us, can we make them? No, we can't. So, essentially, the job of strategy is to make decisions on the things we do control that will compel, we can't force, but it'll compel them. They'll say, gosh, I should take my hard-earned cash, and whether it's a company or an individual, I should take my hard-earned cash and give it to you, rather than give it to nobody, if there's no product now, or give it to a competitive product. So, the important pieces of it is integrated, it's the whole set of choices that has that one outcome, that it compels desired customer action.
turns.zh: 没错。我们希望客户能掏出钱包把钱交给我们，但这根本不可能。战略的核心任务，是在我们可控的领域做出决策，引导客户行动。我们无法强制客户消费，但能通过策略激发他们的购买欲。客户会想：“天哪，我辛辛苦苦赚来的钱，是交给你，还是交给竞争对手？如果现在没有相关产品，我会把钱交给竞争对手。”关键在于，战略是一套相互关联的决策体系，最终目标是促使客户采取理想的行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. And to help people define their strategy, you have something you call the strategy choice cascade, which is basically five questions that you need to answer to help you think trough strategy. Can you talk through this?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。为了帮助人们制定战略，您提出了“战略选择阶梯法”，即需要回答的五个关键问题。能详细讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah. And this is the fruits of many, many years of doing strategy work, and trying to figure out, how do you do this thing? Because the fun thing was, I was in the era, I started in strategy in 1981, and that was early in the era, strategy was born in 1963 with the founding of Boston Consulting Group by Bruce Henderson, who was the father of strategy in my view, of practical commercial strategy. So, it was still in the early days, and Bruce Henderson had a theory of how strategy should... What result it should produce for you. Mike Porter then came along in 1980, so '63 Bruce Anderson, and '80 Porter, the two most important figures in the history of strategy, came along and said, a strategy has to look like this. It has to have this as its output. But neither of them was very good on, because again, it was early, they can't do everything right away, of, well, how would you get one of those? (00:20:34): So, Mike Porter says you have to be either differentiated or low cost. Good. And if you look through competitive strategy as landmark seminal book, to say, how would you do that? There is no answer. And because Monitor Company, the firm I was one of the leaders of for a decade and a half, was founded essentially to commercialize Mike Porter's work, customers would ask us, they'd say, well, we like Mike Porter, and we'd like to have one of those. We can look at ourselves under his framework, and we can say we're stuck in the middle, and he said, that's bad, and he said, good is this or this. How do we think through creating one of those? We didn't actually have an answer. (00:21:22): And it turned out, because I was the most, I don't know, intellectually engaged on this, and didn't mind the hard work of product development from about 1987, when we discovered we really didn't know that, and clients really wanted us to tell them that. Between 1987 and 1995, I did all this work on, well, how could you develop a process for getting yourself one of those, one of those excellent strategies? And I came to the view that you have to have answers to five questions. You have to have an answer to the question of, what's your winning aspiration? What are you trying to accomplish? Because it'll help contextualize the kinds of choices you could make. Then there's a where to play, on what playing field, or if you're like military stuff, battlefield, are you going to plop yourself down on? You're not going to play everywhere, in every product, at every vertical stage around the world, you're going to pick someplace, and in that place, how can you be either better than competitors, in terms of creating customer value, or lower cost than those competitors? (00:22:38): To win there, where you've chosen to play to meet your winning aspirations, what capabilities do you have to have that your competitors don't, that would enable you to win that way? And then, what management systems, enabling management systems, do you have to put in place to make sure you build and maintain those must have capabilities to win, where you've chosen to play, to meet your winning aspiration? And so, I came to the conclusion, actually it was in 1995, the end of an eight-year journey, I came to the conclusion those were the five, and you had to do them together, and that is the essence of producing a strategy that compels desired customer action.
turns.zh: 是的。这正是多年来从事战略工作、努力探寻如何实现这一目标的成果。因为有趣的是，我所在的那个时代——我1981年开始从事战略工作，正值战略诞生的早期阶段。1963年，布鲁斯·亨德森创立波士顿咨询集团，奠定了实用商业战略的理论基础，可以说他是战略之父。所以当时战略仍处于早期阶段，布鲁斯·亨德森提出了战略应达到的成果——即为客户创造特定价值。随后迈克·波特于1980年提出理论，两位战略史上最重要的人物——1963年的布鲁斯·亨德森和1980年的迈克·波特——共同确立了战略的框架与输出标准。但他们都存在局限性，因为当时战略尚处萌芽阶段，无法一蹴而就。比如如何获得这些成果？（00:20:34）波特主张要么实现差异化，要么追求低成本。这很好。但翻阅竞争战略这本里程碑式的著作时，你会发现根本没有标准答案。正因如此，我曾领导的监控公司（Monitor Company）成立的初衷，就是将波特的理论商业化。客户们常问：我们喜欢波特的理论，想要拥有这样的战略。通过他的框架分析后，他们发现自己被困在中间地带，波特说这很糟糕，必须要么追求卓越，要么另辟蹊径。但我们无从下手。（00:21:22）1987年左右，我意识到自己对这项工作最投入，甘愿承受产品开发的艰辛。当时我们发现自己对客户需求知之甚少，而客户又迫切希望我们给出答案。1987至1995年间，我致力于构建一套流程，帮助企业打造卓越战略。最终我总结出五个关键问题：第一，明确你的核心抱负是什么？第二，制定清晰的战略目标。第三，选择合适的战场。第四，构建差异化优势或低成本优势。第五，构建支持战略的管理体系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to go through an example of a company, but before we do that, something I think that's important to talk about is, if your book is called Playing to Win, you talked about this idea of you need to play to win, and you argue that a lot of people are just playing to play, they're playing to play the game. I'm guessing most people listening, and most people developing a strategy, don't think they're doing that, they don't think they're just playing to play the game. They think they're playing to win. I'm curious what are signs that you're not actually playing to win?
turns.zh: 我想以一家公司为例来展开讨论，但在此之前，有一点我认为很重要——如果你写了一本名为《赢者通吃》的书，你提到了“必须为赢而战”的理念，并指出许多人只是为了玩游戏而玩游戏。我猜听众中的大多数人，尤其是制定战略的人，都不会认为自己是这样做的，他们认为自己是在为胜利而战。我很好奇，怎样才能判断自己并非真正在为胜利而战？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: It would be mainly signs given to you by customers. So, if you say, we're the most innovative company in our industry, and customers... And let's say the industry distributes through a given channel, and customers come into that channel and they look at the two products and say, I could flip a coin on this one, you are not effectively playing to win. Maybe you thought you were winning, but customers don't think you are better. Or if your competitor lowers their price compared to your price, and you say to yourself, oh my God, if we lowered our price, we would make no money, but your competitor keeps on pricing there, you may think you have the low cost position, but they do, and you have to give them whatever share they desire at that lower price because you can't compete there. (00:24:56): So, you'll know you're playing to play if you're not aiming to, and accomplishing, having either an offer where Lenny walks into the store, whatever kind of store it is, and says to the person in the store, I want that brand. An example, Lego, one of the companies I've worked with for a long time, great company. It turns out that if you do market research on kids, a store that purports to be a toy store but that doesn't have Lego is not a toy store. They would define it as not a toy. Mom, why are we here? I wanted to go to a toy store. And she said, but it says toys on here. And the kids said, uh-huh. That's an insane brand. That's an insane, insane, insane brand. (00:25:54): And it has a price premium for anything, over any of its competitors by a long shot. It keeps growing, it actually for most years in the last decade it has had 80 or 90% of the entire category growth is Lego. And so, they're playing to win, to be distinctive in the minds of consumers. But Vanguard has got $9 trillion of assets under management last time I checked. Does it do anything distinctive? Not really. The customer bought, do they have the lowest cost position so they can charge the lowest AUMs? Absolutely. And so, there's different kinds of ways, but you'd know by the actions that customers take.
turns.zh: 主要体现在客户给你的反馈上。比如，如果你声称自己是行业中最具创新力的公司，而客户……假设某个行业通过特定渠道分销产品，客户进入这个渠道后看到两款产品时会说：我可以抛硬币决定选哪款。这说明你并没有有效地为胜利而战。或许你自以为赢了，但客户并不认为你更出色。又比如，如果竞争对手降低价格，而你却自言自语：天啊，如果我们也降价就会亏本。但竞争对手却能在低价区间保持定价，你可能认为自己占据了低成本优势，但实际上优势在他们那里。你只能以低价让渡份额，因为你无法在那里竞争。（00:24:56）：所以，如果你不以赢为目标、不实现赢的目标，你就会知道自己在玩游戏。比如，乐高是我长期合作的优秀公司。当你对儿童进行市场调研时，如果一家号称玩具店却没有乐高商品的店铺，孩子们就会说：妈妈，我们要去玩具店。她说：但这儿写着玩具啊。而孩子们说：哼，这品牌太疯狂了。这品牌太疯狂、太疯狂、太疯狂了。（00:25:54）：乐高在价格上远超竞争对手。它持续增长，过去十年间，乐高占据了整个品类80%至90%的增长份额。所以，乐高是在为赢而战，在消费者心目中树立独特形象。而先锋基金上次我查看时管理着9万亿美元资产。它有独特之处吗？没有。客户选择它，是因为它成本最低，可以收取最低的资产管理费吗？绝对是。可见，成功之道各不相同，但从客户行为中就能看出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, essentially, to mirror back what you're saying, to win, there's kind of these two routes you talk about. One is you're the lowest cost option, the second is you're differentiated. You have a differentiated brand, where it's not a coin flip, it's like, oh, I really need that for this reason.
turns.zh: 所以，归根结底，正如你所说，要赢，就有两种路径。一是成为成本最低的选项，二是差异化。拥有差异化品牌，让客户无需犹豫，直接选择：哦，我正需要这个产品，原因是……

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yes. Yeah, you got it.
turns.zh: 是的。没错，你理解得很到位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if you can't do that, then the advice you share is go find a different playing field.
turns.zh: 如果做不到这些，那你的建议就是去寻找另一个竞争领域。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Well, or get out of business, whatever... It's only a matter of time until you're dead, is the sad truth of the matter, which is the competitors in your industry, who are either low cost or differentiated, can essentially jerk you around as much as they want. It's like Southwest Airlines, right? Southwest Airlines was just a tiny little airline that flew Austin, Houston, Dallas, and now it's number one in passenger seat miles in America, and the only airline that's earned its cost of capital over the last half century, all the rest are losing money for their shareholders over time. They have good cycles and bad cycles. How did that happen? Well, it's just the other airlines had to step aside whenever Southwest came into a route, the other airlines just had to say, well, I guess you're going to get your 30 share, or 35 share of passengers on this route, welcome to town. That's all they can do. (00:28:15): They just have to seed position. And that's what happens, if you play to play, you'll end up just being... It's literally like having a bully who can just shove you, and you take one step back, then they shove you, and you take another step back, and they shove you, and you take another step back. There's no way to protect yourself if you're not one of those two. You cannot bully Vanguard, you cannot bully Southwest, you cannot bully Proctor and Gamble, you cannot bully Lego. That's the way the business world works.
turns.zh: 嗯，或者倒闭，反正……你迟早会被淘汰，这是个悲哀的事实。你的行业竞争对手，要么成本低，要么差异化经营，基本上能随意摆布你。这就像西南航空，对吧？西南航空最初只是个小航空公司，服务于奥斯汀、休斯顿和达拉斯，如今却成为美国客运里程数第一的航空公司，也是过去半个世纪唯一一家盈利的航空公司，其余航空公司都一直在给股东带来亏损。它们有好光景，也有坏光景。这是怎么回事呢？嗯，每当西南航空开通一条航线，其他航空公司就不得不让步。其他航空公司只能说，好吧，你在这条航线上能获得30%或35%的客源，欢迎加入。除此之外，他们别无选择。（00:28:15）他们只能先占据有利位置。事情就是这样——如果你想竞争，最终只能成为……简直就像被霸凌者随意欺负，你退一步，他们再推你一把，你再退一步，他们再推你一把。如果你不是那两家巨头之一，就毫无招架之力。你无法霸凌先锋基金（Vanguard），无法霸凌西南航空，无法霸凌宝洁（Proctor and Gamble），无法霸凌乐高（Lego）。这就是商业世界的运行法则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in the case of Southwest, the reason they couldn't be bullied is they were the low cost provider and the other airlines couldn't meet their prices. So, they're like, all right, there's nothing we can do.

turns.zh: 再多说点。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: So, there's a big market over there, we'd like to get some, is a terrible reason in my view. The reason should be, customers are bereft, customers are lacking something that we can provide. This is why I hate... And most entries by foreign companies into China, they get their faces shot off. And the reason is the rationale is, it's big, we could get some of that. So, I don't love it, for starters. And I'm not saying that that'll guarantee failure, but if somebody gave me a review of a pitch deck for that, I would not invest [inaudible 00:43:14].
turns.zh: 所以，那边有一个巨大的市场，我们想分一杯羹，在我看来这是一个糟糕的理由。正确的理由应该是，客户有需求，而我们能提供他们所需。这就是为什么我不喜欢它。大多数外国公司进入中国市场都会碰壁。原因在于他们的逻辑是：市场很大，我们能分一杯羹。所以，一开始我就不太喜欢它。我不是说这一定能导致失败，但如果有人给我一份关于这个项目的Pitch Deck（推介文案），我是不会投资的[00:43:14未听清]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I imagine you can also frame it in other terms, like our customers are demanding more ways to work within Figma with their teams, and there's these-
turns.zh: 嗯，我想你也可以用其他说法来表述，比如我们的客户要求能与他们的团队在Figma中进行更多协作，而那里有这些 -

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah. So, that would be a better one. And you're speculating, I've asked you to speculate, so we don't know. But I like that one better, which is, what's our aspiration? It's to satisfied core customers, who love what we do, but think it's too narrow, that if we could broaden that for them, into this market, our customers would be very happy.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以，那个想法会更好。你现在是在推测，我让你推测的，所以我们还不知道。但我更喜欢那个想法，即我们的愿景是什么？就是要满足核心客户的需求，他们喜欢我们所做的，但认为范围太窄了，如果我们能为他们拓展到这个市场，我们的客户会非常高兴的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really cool. And so, you want to frame it in the words of how customers would benefit, essentially.
turns.zh: 那真是太棒了。所以，你想用客户会受益的词汇来概括本质。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: I just think those tend to be stronger, strongest, if there's a link. Because remember, what is strategy about? Compelling desired customer action. So, everything ties back to that. So, then the where to play would be, you just want to say, okay, what customers are we talking about, or what parts of our current customers that we don't serve are we attempting to serve with that? And with what product? Is it a finished product? Is it a component of a product? Through what distribution channel would we sell this? This is another self-serve type product. I think Figma is mainly self-serve, right? And so, you choose that where, and then say, how can we solve the problem?
turns.zh: 我只是觉得如果能建立联系的话，这些想法往往会更强、更有效。因为记住，战略的核心是什么？就是要激发客户期望的行动。所以，一切都要回归到这一点上。那么，切入点应该是什么呢？你只需要说，好的，我们在谈论哪些客户，或者我们现有客户中哪些未被服务的部分我们打算为他们服务？用什么产品呢？是成品吗？还是产品的一个组件？通过什么分销渠道销售？这又是一个自助服务类产品。我觉得Figma主要就是自助服务，对吧？所以，你选定了切入点，然后再问，我们如何解决这个问题？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we get to that, before we get to that real quick-
turns.zh: 在我们深入探讨之前，先快速说一下——

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, please. Please.
turns.zh: 哦，对，对，对，请说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the things you mentioned there is who specifically are the customers? So, in this case it'd be like product managers, engineers, and other functions, and then there's the distribution channels, how we'd actually get to them?
turns.zh: 那么，你刚才提到的，具体客户是谁？所以，在这种情况下，可能是产品经理、工程师和其他职能部门，然后还有分销渠道，我们如何才能接触到他们？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Get to them, yeah.
turns.zh: 接触到他们，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, what other questions are there within this where we will play?
turns.zh: 那么，在这个切入点上，还有哪些其他问题？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: To what extent is it a finished product or a component? Because sometimes it could be, we'd like to supply this component that could be integrated into other people's products. That's what Apple apps are, right?
turns.zh: 它在多大程度上是成品还是组件？因为有时候可能是，我们想提供一个可以集成到其他人产品中的组件。苹果应用就是这样的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: We don't sell them an iPhone, we sell them a component within the iPhone, a customer's iPhone, is that what we're doing here? Because then you have to ask questions about, well, how does it fit in with the rest?
turns.zh: 我们不是卖给他们iPhone，而是卖给他们iPhone中的一个组件，客户的iPhone，对吧？因为那样的话，你就得问，嗯，它如何与其他部分相契合？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the where also implies where in the product it lives? Where-
turns.zh: 所以，切入点也暗示了它在产品中的位置？在哪里——

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: At what vertical stage? Is it an integrated product, where it's the whole thing from soup to nuts? Is it some upstream pieces that some people downstream? Do we take pieces from other people and assemble them? So, we're the integrator? Those are all important where to play choices, from my view, because those make a big difference. Like Four Seasons chose... Four Seasons the hotel company, luxury hotel, chose a completely different choice on the vertical stage where to play, back in the 80s, they said we're going to get out of real estate development... So buying land and getting it zoned for hotels. We're going to get out of construction, building hotels. We're even going to get out of the business of owning the land or the hotel, so that we can be awesome at hotel management. (00:46:35): Rich people, like Michael Dell, and David Thompson, and Bill Gates will own the hotels, as an investment, and they will be happy to have Four Seasons brand on their hotel, and we will charge a management fee. That is a where to play choice. Even though somebody could say, well, you're a luxury hotel, you're like the other luxury hotels who serve luxury customers at a high price. Oh no, no, no, no, no, they do it with a stack this thick, we do it with a stack this thin.
turns.zh: 处于哪个垂直阶段？是集成产品吗？即从头到尾一站式服务？还是说它只是上游的零部件，供下游的用户使用？我们是否从其他人那里获取零部件然后进行组装？所以，我们是集成商吗？在我看来，选择垂直阶段至关重要，因为这会产生巨大影响。例如，四季酒店（Four Seasons）在上世纪80年代就做出了一个关键的垂直阶段定位选择——退出房地产开发、建筑施工，甚至不再拥有酒店土地或资产，而是专注于酒店管理。（00:46:35）：像迈克尔·戴尔、戴维·汤普森和比尔·盖茨这样的富人会将酒店作为投资项目，并乐意挂上四季品牌，而我们则收取管理费。这就是垂直阶段的定位选择。尽管有人会说，既然你是一家豪华酒店，应该和其他高端品牌一样为富有客户提供高价服务。但不不不，他们的策略截然不同——他们采用厚实的价值链，而我们选择精简的价值链。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, it's like a value chain question. Where in the value chain are you going to play?
turns.zh: 所以这就像一个价值链问题。你要在价值链的哪个环节下注？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Value chain. Yeah. Where in the value chain? That's exactly right. And everybody has value chain questions. They often complain, after the fact, like all the apps complain about what cut Apple is taking, but they made a choice, a value chain choice. We are going to design something that will appear on an iPhone, or an Android device, if it's that case, and then good luck to you. You can complain like crazy that they're taking so much of it, and this is unfair, and they've got to duopoly... Yeah, but you guys cooperated 100% in building that. 100%, never complained about it, until you wanted a bigger piece of the pie. That was a vertical stage, a value chain stage, that you chose, willingly. Nobody forced you to do it.
turns.zh: 价值链。没错。价值链的哪个环节？说得太对了。每个人都会面临价值链的选择问题。他们往往事后抱怨，比如所有应用开发者都在抱怨苹果抽取的高额分成，但这其实是他们自己做出的价值链选择。我们要设计一款能在iPhone或安卓设备上运行的应用，然后，祝你好运吧。如果你抱怨他们抽成太多，那太不公平了，他们还有双头垄断……是啊，但你们当初百分百配合开发了这个应用。百分百，从来没有抱怨过，直到你们想要分得更大一杯羹。这就是你们主动选择的垂直阶段、价值链阶段。没人强迫你们这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And Apple's not playing ball, giving it back too easily.
turns.zh: 而苹果可不会轻易让步。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: No. No. And do I love just how controlling and everything Apple is? Do I? No, but would I say, oh, those poor apps, right? Yeah, no, get your own distribution channel, buddy.
turns.zh: 不不不。我是否欣赏苹果这种强势控制一切的作风？我不欣赏，但我会说，哦，那些可怜的应用开发者啊，对吧？是啊，不行，自己去找分销渠道吧，伙计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cold blooded.
turns.zh: 冷酷无情。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so we've talked about the winning aspirations, so for FigJam, it would be satisfy customers that are trying to work with their team in these different ways, and make sure they're staying, make sure they get what they need out of Figma, versus go maybe to other tools. And then, where will we play? Let's say, engineers, product managers is trying to target them, distribution through the existing product, and so it's like a feature of the existing product. And then, it's how will we win? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 好的，我们已经讨论了赢利目标，那么对于FigJam来说，就是要满足那些试图以不同方式与团队协作的客户，确保他们留存下来，从Figma获得所需的价值，而非转向其他工具。那么，我们该如何定位？比如，工程师、产品经理就是我们的目标客户，通过现有产品进行分发，所以这就像现有产品的某个功能特性。那么，我们如何取胜？你们怎么看？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Well, you ask the question, how can we solve... Well, how can we either solve that problem at a much lower cost, so we can always be a sharper price point than them? So, if there are solutions, but they cost 50,000 a user because their costs are 30,000 a user, we can do this for $15 a user, and so we can charge $100 per seat, and absolutely annihilate the competitor by figuring out a less costly way to do it. Or there are other selections, but they make the user do all these things, and it's ponderous, and it takes a long time... We have shortcuts, we use AI to, you just say a few words into it, and they say, oh yeah, I know what you mean, and here it goes in the workflow. (00:49:54): Or we're more integrated, like Thomson Reuters, the company I was on the board of, our advantage was we were better integrated into the workflow. You didn't have to get out of your workflow to go use this product, and then you get back in, we just said, what's your workflow? Oh, well, integrated. Is it better integrated into their workflow that makes their life easier? It would be questions, possibilities like that that I would be asking. Essentially, you've got to have a theory there, of how are you going to be better or lower cost.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。你问这个问题，我们怎么解决……嗯，我们怎样才能以更低的成本解决这个问题，这样我们就能始终比他们更具价格优势？所以，如果有解决方案，但每个用户成本是5万美元，而他们的成本是3万美元，我们就能以每用户15美元的价格做到这一点，然后每个席位收费100美元，彻底击败竞争对手，只要我们能找到成本更低的解决方案。或者其他方案会让用户做很多事，而且流程繁琐，耗时很久……我们有捷径，比如用AI，你只需对它说几句话，它就会说：“哦，对，我明白你的意思，接着就进入工作流程了。”（00:49:54）：或者我们更集成化，比如我曾在董事会任职的汤森路透，我们的优势在于更好地集成到工作流程中。用户无需离开当前工作流程去使用我们的产品，再重新切换回来，我们只需问：“你的工作流程是怎样的？”“哦，集成度很高。”“那它与他们的工作流程相比，是否更易用？” 这类问题和可能性正是我会思考的。本质上，你得有自己的理论，思考如何才能更出色或更具成本优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On the lower cost front, I think generally the advice is you don't want to go that route, that's a very difficult route. What's your thinking of just when to go that route that you might actually win at lower costs?
turns.zh: 在降低成本方面，我认为一般建议是别走这条路，因为这条路太难了。你什么时候该走这条路才能真正在成本上取胜？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: That's not advice I give. I think they're both completely legitimate strategies. They have implications. So, if you want to be the cost leader, it is rare that you can be the cost leader without having dominant scale in the territory in which you're operating. So, if you want to be a niche cost leader, good luck to you, that's almost never going to happen. So, Vanguard had to make a race to, we're going to do index mutual funds, and it doesn't exist now, we're going to do it and we're going to get gigantic, and we can't let anybody get close to us in size because we want to have the lowest cost position. And so, they are the world's biggest mutual fund company, and you have to do that, and same with Southwest, to really make that model work, they had to keep expanding and expanding to get bigger. (00:51:45): M&M Mars... It takes an enormous amount of commitment to say, we're going to go, and we're just going to keep charging ahead on this. Whereas, in differentiation, I think you can differentiate sometimes at lower scale, and build yourself slowly towards higher scale. But the business world is just getting so much more scale sensitive. When you think about the costs of differentiation, it's often spending on branding, spending on R&D, R&D innovation. Those two are of the most scale sensitive elements of anybody's cost structure. And so, being a niche-y differentiator is getting harder and harder in my view.
turns.zh: 这不是我给出的建议。我认为这两种策略都完全合理，都有其影响。如果你想成为成本领先者，除非你在运营区域拥有主导规模，否则很难做到。因此，如果你想成为利基成本领先者，祝你好运，这几乎永远不可能实现。例如，先锋基金（Vanguard）必须发起一场竞赛：我们要做指数共同基金，现在这种产品还不存在，但我们要去做，要做大，要确保没人能在规模上接近我们，因为我们想占据最低成本的位置。于是他们成了全球最大的共同基金公司。你必须这样做，西南航空（Southwest）也是如此，要让这种模式奏效，他们必须不断扩张壮大。（00:51:45）：玛氏（M&M Mars）……要说我们要勇往直前，这需要巨大的决心。而在差异化方面，我认为有时你可以在较小规模上实现差异化，然后慢慢发展到更大规模。但商业世界对规模的敏感度越来越高。当你考虑差异化的成本时，往往涉及品牌投入、研发投入、创新投入。这些是任何成本结构中最受规模影响的两个方面。因此，在我看来，成为利基型差异化者越来越难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's also important to say, either path is very hard, it's very hard to build a business that makes money and is profitable and survives just broadly.
turns.zh: 我认为同样重要的是，要说无论哪条路都很难，要建立一个能赚钱、盈利且能广泛存续的企业实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yes, yes, I agree.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，我同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're not going to have this formula of how to win, okay, we got it. We got a big business.
turns.zh: 而且你不会有那种公式化的成功之道，说“好，我们做到了。我们做成了大生意。”

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: I agree. I agree. And that's why, if I looked at 100 strategies of major companies, I'd say I didn't like 90 of them very much.
turns.zh: 我同意。我同意。所以，如果我审视100家大公司的战略，我会说其中90个我都不太喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, the other nine out of 10 probably look good, but also don't work out.
turns.zh: 然后，另外十分之九的战略可能看起来不错，但最终也不见得能成功。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yes. Yeah, no, that's true. There's lots of spaghetti thrown at lots of walls in the world of business.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，没错。这就是商业世界里"撞南墙"的现象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, capitalism.
turns.zh: 对啊，资本主义。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, now we're at the capability step of trying to figure out what capabilities you need to win. Can you talk about, say with FigJam, what are the sorts of things you think about here?
turns.zh: 好的。那么，现在我们来到了能力层面，试图弄清楚你需要哪些能力才能获胜。你能谈谈，比如用FigJam这样的工具，你在这里会考虑哪些方面的问题？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Well, I guess I'd ask myself questions, like, is there a learning curve to this, where we could have better capabilities because we started earlier than anybody else, and have more essentially cumulative experience? Is there a way that we've figured out how to serve customers that make them feel tended to better by us? So, we've got helpline... We figured out how to do the helpline, because if it's self-serve and that's how they get the product, and then they've got issues with how to use it, they feel that we're just better. We're the best of all their providers at that. How to win is a theory of how customers are going to perceive us better, if we're differentiated. And then, it's what capabilities would we have to have to make that theory come true, rather than just be a wish. So, if we want them to feel like we're the easiest to deal with, we have to have capabilities to do that. (00:54:47): It's just like again, Four Seasons said the reason they're by far and away the most successful, profitable, best in all fronts, luxury hotel chain in the world... Biggest, best, most profitable, best employee rankings, best guest rankings, all of those. Well, their how to win was they said, people, if you talk to people who are in luxury hotels, they'd rather not be there. You'd say, wow, they're in the lap of luxury, why would that be? Where do you think they'd prefer to be, Lenny?
turns.zh:
嗯，我想我会问自己一些问题，比如，这是否存在一个学习曲线？我们是否因为比其他人更早起步、积累了更多经验而拥有更好的能力？是否有某种方法能让我们更好地服务客户，让他们感觉我们更贴心？比如，我们设置了帮助热线……我们想出了如何运营帮助热线，因为如果用户是自助服务获取产品，然后遇到使用问题，他们会觉得我们更出色，是他们所有供应商中最好的。如何获胜的核心在于，如何让客户因为我们的差异化而更认可我们。然后，我们需要具备哪些能力才能让这个理论成为现实，而不仅仅是空想。比如，如果我们想让客户觉得我们最容易打交道，就必须具备实现这一目标的能力。
（00:54:47）：再比如，四季酒店称自己是迄今为止最成功、最赚钱、各方面表现最佳的豪华酒店连锁……规模最大、利润最高、员工满意度最高、客户满意度最高等等。他们的成功秘诀是，他们说，如果问在豪华酒店住过的人，他们宁愿不在那里住。你可能会惊讶，他们明明身处奢华之中，为什么还会这么想？你觉得他们更愿意住哪里，莱尼？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: At home.
turns.zh: 在家。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah. Dominantly at home, for their segment, which was high-end business travelers. They've traveled, they've stayed in one luxury hotel too many 20 years ago. And so, we're going to have luxury defined as not grand architecture and decor and [inaudible 00:55:38] service, but rather, we're going to define it as a service that makes up for what you left at home or at the office. (00:55:44): Because people would rather be, if they have to not be at home, they'd rather be at the office than in a hotel because they can be more productive. So, we need capabilities, we need staff that can deliver on that capability. What's the problem, for that? The problem is turnover in the hotel industry globally is 80% a year, which means that the average person you meet, the average staff person you meet in the average hotel, is on their way to a 16-month career at that hotel chain. So, how do you deliver that really cool special kind of service with that? The answer is... And now I'm skipping ahead to enabling management systems. (00:56:26): You have to have a different way of recruiting, a different way of onboarding, a different way of career development. And if you do all of those things, you end up with a 10% turnover rate, so that your people are there 10 years on average, and you can then get them trained up to deliver that kind of service. So, that's the capability that you build, and the people, to be able to take more decision-making at a lower level, and treat the guests in a customized way that makes them feel that this wasn't by the book, some rule book, that this person just said, no, this is a good solution for my guest.
turns.zh: 是的。他们主要面向高端商务旅客群体，在国内市场占据主导地位。这些旅客过去20年里住过太多豪华酒店。因此，我们对豪华的定义不应局限于宏伟的建筑、奢华的装饰和[00:55:38处语音不清]服务，而应将其定义为能弥补人们在家或办公室所缺失的体验。（00:55:44）因为如果人们不得不离开家乡，他们宁愿待在办公室而非酒店，因为在办公室能更高效地工作。因此，我们需要具备相应能力的员工。问题出在哪里？全球酒店业每年人员流动率高达80%，这意味着你在普通酒店遇到的员工平均只会在该连锁酒店工作16个月。那么如何在这种情况下提供优质的个性化服务呢？答案是……接下来我要讲的是赋能管理系统。（00:56:26）你必须采用不同的招聘方式、入职流程和职业发展机制。若能做好这些工作，人员流动率可降至10%，员工平均服务期达10年，这样才能通过培训让他们提供卓越的服务。关键在于建立赋能管理体系，让员工能自主决策，以个性化方式对待客人，让客人感受到服务并非按部就班、遵循规则，而是服务者根据实际情况为其量身定制解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that these capabilities and even the management systems, which is step five, relate to your moat. Which is the thing you need to achieve, also, ideally is the thing that other people, it'll make it hard for them to do.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这些能力甚至包括管理系统（第五步），都与你的护城河息息相关。护城河是企业必须具备的核心竞争力，理想情况下，其他企业很难复制。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yep. So, you're exactly right. You can call if you want, how to win, moat, right? Definition of your moat. And so, capabilities and management systems are what both build and maintain the moat, and the maintaining is an important part because if you are the most successful, people are going to say, I want to do that too. But here's where there's this modern, unfortunately, bull shitty thing that says, oh, competitive advantage is fleeting in this modern hyper-competitive world, and you can't have long-term advantage anymore. And I just say, oh, I see. So, Four Seasons, I guess that isn't very long-term, that has only been 45 years now, since they... No, 35 years I should say. Don't exaggerate. Since they went to that strategy. Oh, and Tide. So, 77 years isn't a long time, I guess either, because they've been the number one detergent for 77 consecutive years. I guess you're right, it's fleeting. (00:58:16): It's not. But what makes it fleeting is when you have one thing, and one thing only. So, let's say you build the biggest polyethylene plant in the world, near a good feedstock source, and you have the low cost position, what's somebody else going to do when they see how much money you make doing that? Build a polyethylene plant beside yours, twice the size, and then you're toast. Why? Because the competitive advantage was too simple. But at Four Seasons, you got to sell off all your hotels, you got to fire all the people involved in hotel development and everything, and actually, the people in the business like doing that, you have to essentially get rid of your entire staff, start from scratch, paying them more than you do now by far, giving them more career security, giving them more training, giving them better uniforms, whatever, spending 10 times as much hiring them, with the hopes that maybe someday you'll be able to produce the kind of services Four Seasons does. (00:59:24): The competitors basically say, life's too short. Do they give up and die? No, there are other great chains, Mandarin Oriental, my wife loves staying in Mandarin Oriental, even more than Four Seasons often. But they've not said, we will replicate Four Seasons, they've said, we'll pick a different where, and a different how, and that's, in the end, what you want. Is rather than complete overlap, where you've got concentric circles of people picking the same where, you convince people to pick different wheres. That's why people sort of say, Roger, how to win, that's so impolitic, because you're producing losers, and then there's victims, and all that. There's oppressor and oppressive. It fits in the modern dialogue. And I say, no, what I want to do is encourage them to find someplace else to prosper, rather than smash on top of us. (01:00:27): And so, if you have completely different capabilities and management systems, it'll encourage people to choose a different where to play, how to win. If your capabilities and management systems are very similar to your competitors, and you're succeeding with your chosen where to play, how to win, what are they going to do? They're going to drive straight to your where to play and try to win exactly the same place and wreck your market for both of you. That's what you don't want. And the more complicated, in some sense... I shouldn't use complicated. The more nuanced and multifaceted your capabilities and management systems are, the more likely they're going to say life's too short. That's what everybody says about Southwest. So, if you're the only airline in the United States that's earning its cost of capital for 50 years, wouldn't you say, gee, I'd love to be like that? But what does it mean? (01:01:29): Well, it means selling off most of your aircraft, so that you can have only one kind of aircraft, 737. Tearing up your entire root structure, your entire hub and spoke structure, and make it point to point. Changing your complete labor relations strategy, from fighting the unions to paying them a lot, as long as they're highly flexible. People think Southwest is non-union, it's not unionized [inaudible 01:01:55], but they do different... You have to essentially fire all your travel agents, and convince your customers to book online, by themselves, to save more money. Life's too short, it's just too short. So, they try things like Continental Light, or Ted, that do half the things that Southwest does, and then you're what? A crappy Southwest. So, to me, that's the ultimate. The ultimate is, it's like the ultimate weapon is the one you never use. The ultimate way to compete to win is to never actually be forced to compete.
turns.zh:
是的。所以你说得完全正确。如果你想知道如何取胜、护城河之类的，对吧？护城河的定义。能力和管理体系是建立和维护护城河的关键，而维护护城河至关重要，因为如果你是最成功的，人们就会说，"我也想这么做"。但现在有个现代的、可悲的胡说八道的观点，认为在竞争激烈的现代世界里，竞争优势转瞬即逝，无法再保持长期优势。我就想说，那好吧，比如四季酒店，我猜他们的护城河也不算持久，毕竟他们只经营了45年——不，应该是35年，别夸大其词。从他们采用那个战略开始。还有汰渍洗衣粉。77年也不算长吧，因为他们连续77年都是洗衣粉市场第一。我想你说得对，确实转瞬即逝。（00:58:16）但关键在于，当你只有一种方法、一种策略时，竞争对手就会模仿。比如你建了全球最大的聚乙烯工厂，靠近优质原料来源，占据低成本优势，但当别人看到你赚得盆满钵满时，他们会怎么做？建个规模两倍的工厂来竞争，那你就完蛋了。为什么？因为你的竞争优势太简单了。但四季酒店呢？你得卖掉所有酒店，解雇所有参与酒店开发的人员——说真的，业内人士乐此不疲——几乎要彻底重组团队，远超现有薪资标准，提供更好的职业保障和培训，换上更优质的制服，投入十倍人力成本招聘新员工，只为重现四季的服务水准。（00:59:24）竞争对手会说，人生苦短。他们会放弃吗？不，还有其他优秀连锁，比如文华东方，我妻子甚至比喜欢四季更爱住文华东方。但他们从不模仿四季，而是另辟蹊径，选择不同的战略方向和实施路径。这才是关键。与其让人们在同一战场上竞争，不如说服他们另辟蹊径。这就是人们说"罗杰，你怎么能教人如何取胜？"显得不近人情的原因——因为你是在制造输家和受害者，还有压迫者和被压迫者。这符合现代话语体系。我说，不，我想鼓励他们另辟蹊径，而不是在我们头上横加压迫。（01:00:27）所以，如果你拥有完全不同的能力和管理体系，就会鼓励人们选择不同的战略方向和取胜之道。若你的能力和管理体系与竞争对手高度相似，却又在既定战略上取得成功，他们会怎么做？他们会直奔你的战场，试图复制你的成功，把市场拱手相让。这正是你不愿看到的。而从某种意义上说……我不该用"复杂"这个词。你的能力和管理体系越细致入微、多面化，他们就越容易说，人生苦短。这就是人们对西南航空的看法。所以，如果你是美国唯一一家50年来都能赚回资本成本的航空公司，
多年来，你难道不会想，天哪，我真想成为那样啊？但这意味着什么？（01:01:29）嗯，这意味着要卖掉大部分飞机，只留下一种机型——737。彻底拆解整个航线网络和枢纽辐射结构，转而采用点对点模式。彻底改变劳资关系策略，从与工会抗争转向高薪留人，只要他们足够灵活。人们以为西南航空是非工会的，但其实并非如此[01:01:55]，他们只是采取了不同的策略……你得解雇所有旅行社代理，迫使客户自己在线预订以节省成本。人生太短暂了，实在是太短暂了。所以，他们尝试推出像大陆航空轻便版（Continental Light）或Ted Airlines这样的产品，这些公司只做西南航空一半的业务，那又怎样？不过是个劣质的西南航空罢了。对我来说，这才是终极秘诀。终极武器，往往是永远不用的那把。终极竞争制胜之道，就是永远不必被迫卷入竞争。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's a great quote. This story about Southwest makes me think about Hamilton Helmer's counter-positioning, I don't know if you've heard that term, but basically, you position yourself in a way where the competitor can't do the thing that you're doing because of the way their business is already structured.
turns.zh: 哇，这句话太妙了。南方航空的这个案例让我联想到汉密尔顿·赫尔默提出的反向定位策略。不知道你有没有听过这个术语，但简单来说，就是通过巧妙设计，让竞争对手无法复制你的策略，因为他们的业务结构存在天然壁垒。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Ah, that's sounds right. The can't.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实没法模仿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, can't.
turns.zh: 对啊，他们做不到。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: The can't thing. Awesome. Yeah, and Mike Porter, and he may quote Mike on that, Mike was very big on that. He said, it's fault lines. You're trying to find fault line, where it is so painful for your competitor to come across that fault line, into your side. And so, a great example of that would be Olay, at P&G, and it's in the book, when we did the repositioning of that. The competitor that could have killed us, absolutely killed us, was Estée Lauder with Clinique. If they would've brought Clinique into the mass channels... Because we were doing a Clinique kind of thing, in the mass channels, rather than the prestige. Prestige is like the first four of the department stores, which [inaudible 01:03:51] or Sephora, or Ulta. If Estée Lauder would've taken their Clinique brand and brought it into mass, they would've killed what we were doing. Simple as that. (01:04:05): And in fact, Clinique was the biggest brand in all of skincare, we became the biggest brand in all of skincare, and they didn't do it. Why? Are they idiots? No, they're not, Estée Lauder's super smart. But Estée Lauder also has Bobby Brown, and Mac, and the Estée Lauder, its own brand, and a half a dozen more, all in prestige, and the prestige channel, if they'd have taken Clinique, and taken it over into mass, would've done what? Shot them in the face. Killed them, right? They would've been just apoplectic. And so, Estée Lauder had to stay... If that's counter-positioning by Helmer's terms. They had to stay there. Was that stupid? No, they're still, with all of their brands combined, the biggest in skincare. But Clinique has lost leadership to our brand that they would've considered kind of nothing. Oil of Olay became Olay Olay ProV, Regenerist, all of these higher priced products than they could ever imagine being sold in the mass channel. But our biggest friend was, in some sense, their distribution channel, which would've killed them if we... Literally. They would've just punished them so, so, so bad that they didn't do it.
turns.zh: 就是那个没法模仿的点。太棒了。还有迈克·波特，他可能提到过这个观点。迈克对此深有研究。他说，市场竞争就像断层线。你要找到一个让竞争对手难以跨越的断层线，把他们引入你的阵营。比如宝洁的玉兰油品牌。书里有详细案例，当时我们重新定位玉兰油品牌时，本可以将其击垮的竞争对手是雅诗兰黛旗下的倩碧品牌。如果雅诗兰黛把倩碧引入大众市场……因为我们当时在大众市场做倩碧产品，而雅诗兰黛主打的是高端市场，比如百货公司前四档、丝芙兰、Ulta等专卖店。雅诗兰黛若把倩碧引入大众市场，肯定能毁掉我们的业务。就是这么简单。（01:04:05）事实上，倩碧曾是护肤品市场领导者，我们后来也成为护肤品领域的领军者，但雅诗兰黛没有这么做。为什么？他们是傻瓜吗？不，雅诗兰黛非常聪明。但雅诗兰黛旗下还有Bobby Brown、Mac等品牌，以及雅诗兰黛自身品牌，全部定位于高端市场。如果把倩碧引入大众市场，肯定会自毁前程。雅诗兰黛不得不坚守原有定位。这是反向定位策略吗？没错，他们必须坚守原有定位。这算不算愚蠢？不，他们所有品牌加起来仍是护肤品市场的巨头。但倩碧已将领导地位拱手让给我们这个曾被他们视为微不足道的品牌。玉兰油后来推出了玉兰油专业系列、再生系列等高价产品，远超他们想象的能在大众市场销售的价格。但我们的最大盟友其实是他们的分销渠道，如果我们……真的引入他们的分销渠道，肯定能重创他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that I'm learning all this strategic thinking about makeup and skincare, I also love just the idea of you leading strategy for skincare and makeup brands.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢学到这些关于美妆和护肤品的战略思维了，也喜欢你主导护肤品和美妆品牌战略的经历。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah, no, I got Proctor & Gamble into color cosmetics.
turns.zh: 是的，没错，我成功让宝洁进军彩妆市场了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So funny. [inaudible 01:05:51] love that. I don't know if you're following the AI Google stuff that's happening, where there's search engines competing with Google by just answering the question versus giving you a bunch of blue links?
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。（01:05:51）我喜欢这个想法。不知道你是否关注谷歌的人工智能项目，他们推出了只需回答问题而非提供蓝色链接的搜索引擎，正在与谷歌竞争？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's this question of, we'll Google Shift because people seem to really like it, versus they're making trillions of dollars running ads when they share blue links, and it's this super innovator's dilemma position they're in.
turns.zh: 还有个问题，我们可以谷歌“Shift”，因为人们似乎很喜欢这个功能，但他们通过蓝色链接投放广告赚得盆满钵满，这真是创新者的困境。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Yeah, no, no, I am very interested in what's going on in AI, and I'm writing some stuff on that. But it's hard. I've seen the inside of this for many of my clients, it is super hard when the guts of how you make money is under threat, and you just don't want that thing to go away. The big auto OEMs make money selling cars with ice engines, it's simple as that. And there's no surprise, they've been doing it for 100 years, they're way down the learning curve, they have scale, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. And so, these damn electric vehicles are kind of no fun. And so, the Google situation you've described, I think it's similar. But my general advice is always the same, which is, it can take a while, but in the end the customers will triumph. And A.G. Lafley, my friend who I co-wrote the book with, great CEO, was very good on this. And one of his big customers, big [inaudible 01:07:27] customers came to him and said, if you don't stop cooperating with Amazon, we're going to de-list all your products. (01:07:35): Big threat. Big threat. And A.G. just said, "If customers want to shop there, we just can't not be where our customers want to shop. And so, if you feel you need to do that, you're going to have to, because customers want to shop there, and we are not doing that. But what are you offended by, that we're doing there?" And they said, "Well, you are allowing them to ship products to their customers from your distribution centers." And A.G. just said, "Yeah? Do you want to too?" And they were like... And he just said, "We don't do anything special for them that we wouldn't do for you, they ask for things that you don't ask for because of their business model. But if you come to us with ideas of how we can help you serve our joint customers better, we're all in. But we're not boycotting a place that customers have shown they want to shop," as long as it's an honest, if Amazon was sleazy and dishonest or whatever, but an honest, upstanding place where customers can get our products. (01:09:06): And so, that's where I'm at, which is, you may have to scramble like hell, you may have to suffer from economic downturn, but if you think you can... I always think of it, I don't know if you did this as a kid, Lenny, but when we went to the beach on family trips, we would, I have four brothers, we would build... Plus then a baby girl later. But we would build sand castles and try to hold back the tide, this would be in Florida or California, and we'd try and hold back the tide, and we'd come the next morning to see if our castle... And it was always gone. It's gone. But we'd keep trying doing it, and it's sort of like, you can't hold back the tide. Maybe you can for a while, but you can't forever. So, you just have to figure out where are the customers going. And if they're going someplace... (01:10:07): And Vanguard did this, Jack Bogle, the late Jack Bogle, he died now, a couple of years ago now, he did not like ETFs. He said ETFs are not as good for customers as mutual funds. And he had all sorts of good reasons for that, but the index ETF business started to grow like crazy, and Jack had to relent and say, I don't think it's good for them, but they want it, and so they went whole hog into it, and are the leading index ETF provider, as well as the index mutual fund provider. But for a while they weren't, but he realized it was the tide, and he was attempting to hold back the tide. So, good luck. Good luck to you on that. So, to me, if Google thinks they can, because of their power and the fact they've got a multi-trillion dollar market cap, and they've got a near monopoly position on something, they can hold back the tide. (01:11:09): You see, the water finds a way to flow. Think about Microsoft and its monopoly on PC operating systems, or it's near monopoly on PC operating systems. And I would argue that they abuse that kind of monopoly. I often asked people, when's the last Windows update that got you as a customer excited?
turns.zh:
是的，不，不，我对人工智能领域的发展很感兴趣，也写过一些相关文章。但这真的很难。我为许多客户深入研究过这个领域，当你赖以赚钱的核心业务受到威胁时，那种恐惧感真是难以承受。你就是不想让这种威胁消失。大型汽车制造商靠销售内燃机汽车赚钱，就这么简单。毫不奇怪，他们在这一领域深耕百年，积累了深厚的经验和规模优势。电动汽车这种新兴技术实在令人头疼。就拿谷歌的案例来说，我觉得情况类似。不过我的总体建议始终如一：客户终将胜出。我的好友A.G.拉夫利（A.G. Lafley）曾是宝洁公司的CEO，他对此深有体会。有一位大客户（具体名字未提及）威胁要下架所有产品，除非谷歌停止与亚马逊合作。A.G.冷静回应："如果客户想在亚马逊购物，我们就必须在那里出现。你们想封杀我们的产品？那就尽管试试。"对方反问："那你允许亚马逊用你们的配送中心向客户发货呢？"A.G.反问："是吗？那你也想这么做吗？"对方支吾其词，A.G.最后说："只要亚马逊是诚信经营的平台，我们就无所谓。但如果你们想用商业模式优势来压榨我们，那我们绝不退让。"

（01:09:06）：这就是我的看法。你们可能得拼命应变，可能会遭遇经济低迷，但只要你们相信自己能突破阻碍……我记得小时候和家人去海滩玩，我们四个兄弟，还有后来出生的妹妹，会堆沙堡，试图阻挡潮水。但第二天早晨，沙堡总会消失。潮水不可阻挡。或许短暂抵挡，但终究无法永久抗拒。所以关键在于识别客户的需求方向。只要他们朝着某个方向前进……

（01:10:07）：先锋基金（Vanguard）就是个例子。已故基金经理杰克·博格尔（Jack Bogle）曾反对ETF，认为它们不如共同基金友好。但ETF业务如火如荼，博格尔最终不得不妥协，成为ETF和共同基金领域的领军者。起初他们抵制，但最终顺势而为。谷歌也应该这样做。凭借其市场影响力和数万亿美元的规模，谷歌或许能暂时延缓变革，但终将被客户需求所推动。
比如说，如果一家公司占据了某个领域的近乎垄断地位，他们就能遏制住市场扩张的势头。（01:11:09）：你看啊，水总能找到流淌的路径。想想微软在个人电脑操作系统领域的垄断地位，或者说近乎垄断的地位。我认为他们滥用了这种垄断权力。我常问人们，最近一次让你们这些用户感到兴奋的Windows更新是什么时候？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, Windows 95.
turns.zh: 是的，Windows 95。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: The answer, I think is really clear, Windows 95, right?
turns.zh: 答案，我觉得很明显，就是Windows 95，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Because that's when he took the graphical user interface that he bought rights to from Steve Jobs and put it on, so you didn't have to do backslash backslash... You could actually point and click. That's a long time ago, last time I checked, that's now almost 30 years. And so, they just abused their customer. Is their share of PC operating systems much lower than it was then? No. But that's not the right measure of share. The right measure of share in my view in that industry is your share of minutes spent staring at a smart screen. That's what the share of operating systems that you should care about. And so, what kind of smart screens do people now stare at most? Most? And what other one do a lot of people stare at who really like them? Pads. And so, if you added up all those and said, what do you think... So, what's their share of smartphone operating systems? Microsoft? (01:12:55): Last time I checked it was 0.4 of 1%. Yeah, so effectively zero. How about pads? Apparently it's 4% there. So, their share of people staring at a smart screen has plummeted. Plummeted. Why? Because water finds its own level. People said, there are these other ways of getting around this, and I'm going to take those ways. And I think the degree to which people use their smartphone for more things, as the function of that smartphone is advanced so much faster than your PC operating system, because more people are using it. So, that's what I'd say to Google. I don't care how painful it is, water flows downhill, the tide comes in, and you cannot stop that, even if you're one of the most powerful three firms on the face of the planet.
turns.zh: 因为那时候他把从史蒂夫·乔布斯那里买来的图形用户界面（GUI）放了进去，这样你就不用输入回车键了……你可以直接点击操作了。那已经是很久以前的事了，上次我查过，现在已经快30年了。所以，他们就是在欺负用户。他们的PC操作系统市场份额现在比那时低很多了吗？没有。但这不是衡量份额的正确标准。在我看来，衡量份额的正确标准应该是用户在智能屏幕上花费的时间份额。这才是你应该关注的操作系统份额。那么，现在人们最常盯着哪种智能屏幕？大多数人？还有哪种设备让很多人喜欢到愿意盯着看？平板电脑。所以，如果把这些加起来，再问你怎么看……那么，他们在智能手机操作系统上的份额是多少？微软？（01:12:55）：上次我查过，是0.4%。这基本上就是零了。那平板电脑呢？显然是4%。所以，他们盯着智能屏幕的人数急剧下降了。急剧下降。为什么？因为水往低处流。人们会说，还有其他方法可以解决这个问题，我就要用那些方法。我认为随着智能手机功能的快速发展，以及更多人使用它，人们用智能手机做的事情比用PC操作系统多得多。所以，这就是我想对谷歌说的。我不在乎这有多痛苦，水往低处流，潮水上涨，你即使是地球上最强大的三家公司之一也无法阻止这一趋势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it may take time, but eventually the customer tide pulls, that's a, I think that's really important.
turns.zh: 这可能需要时间，但最终客户的潮流会推动变化，我认为这真的很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I want to end with one very tactical question for people, that may feel overwhelmed, they're just like, oh my God, I don't know what we're going to do, this is so hard, all strategy stuff. You have this really cool idea called betterment, I think you wrote a media post about it, thinking betterment over perfection. And it gives you a first step of like, okay, here's a way to move forward. Can you just talk about that approach?
turns.zh: 是的。我想以一个非常实际的问题结束，对那些可能感到不知所措的人来说，他们可能会想，天哪，我不知道该做什么，这太难了，全是战略层面的东西。你有一个很酷的概念叫做“改进”，我记得你写过一篇媒体文章，主张“优先考虑改进而非完美”。它给了你一个第一步，比如，好的，这里有一种前进的方法。你能谈谈这种方法吗？

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: So, for me, strategy, this thing called strategy, with people, oh my God, oh my God, how am I going to do strategy? Whatever. I just think of it as a problem solving tool. And what problem should you attempt to solve? You should attempt to solve something where your current outcomes that you're getting are lower than the outcomes you wish you were getting. That's what I call a gap. There's a gap between those two. And you should just conceptualize it as, your current outcomes are a natural result of all the choices you've made interacting with the competitive environment. And so, you should reasonably assume that probably those outcomes aren't going to get a whole lot better, because they are the way they are for a good reason. So, you're going to need to make a different set of choices to make that gap go away. That's what I would work on. (01:15:31): I would just ask the question, what is the single most painful gap currently that I'm facing? Customers used to do this, and they're doing this, I can't find this kind of resources, our distribution channel has abandoned us... Whatever is the most painful thing, and then just tackle that. And say, what different choices could I make? And I'd say, use my cascade. Could I change where I'm playing? Could I change how I'm winning? Could I change my capabilities? Could I change my manage systems, in order to achieve a different aspiration? And so, don't try to solve the problems of the world, or even all the problems of your company, that's perfection. Betterment is making that gap go away. And guess what happens if you make that gap go away? You can turn your attention to the next gap, and the next gap, and the next gap. (01:16:28): And if you do that all the time, you're always working on the next gap, the next... They'll get smaller and smaller over time. I don't know if this is a great analogy, but I was dean of a business school for 15 years, the guy who won the professor of the year award more times than anybody else, and did it sort of teaching tough courses, often executive MBA courses, and the like, had a simple formula for doing it. Which is, he taught second-year courses, and second-year courses happened to be 13 two hour lectures, or sessions, [inaudible 01:17:10] or another. He just polled the students on what they thought of each session as they went along, and regardless of the reason, regardless of anything else, simply chopped number 13 every year. (01:17:26): Because in some sense, it's the biggest gap, the gap between what the customers, students, wished for, and were getting. And he would just replace it with something. He would try something else, and replace it with that. And you'd say, and that gets you professor of the year every year? And the answer is yes, betterment. Because if you're teaching for 25 years and you just keep doing that every year, every year, the course keeps getting better and better and better and better and better and better. So, betterment, it doesn't make purists feel awesome, but I'm not here to make purists feel awesome, I'm here to help people get better.
turns.zh: 对我来说，战略——这个所谓的战略，与人打交道时，天哪，天哪，我该怎么做战略呢？无所谓啦。我只把它看作是一个解决问题的工具。那么，你应该尝试解决什么样的问题呢？你应该去解决当前成果低于期望目标的那个问题。那就是我所说的"差距"。两者之间存在着差距。你可以把它理解为：你目前的成果是与竞争环境互动后所做选择的自然结果。因此，你应该合理地假设，这些结果不太可能大幅改善，因为它们之所以是现在这个样子，肯定是有充分理由的。所以，你需要做出不同的选择来消除这个差距。这才是我会关注的重点。（01:15:31）我会先问自己：我目前面临的最痛苦的差距是什么？客户曾经这样做，现在还在这样做；我找不到这样的资源；我们的分销渠道抛弃了我们……无论什么最让人痛苦的事，都应该先解决它。然后问自己：我能做出哪些不同的选择？我会用我的“瀑布模型”来分析。能否改变我的行动场域？能否改变我的获胜方式？能否提升我的能力？能否优化我的管理系统，以实现不同的愿景？所以，不要试图解决世界的问题，甚至公司所有的问题，那是完美主义。进步，就是消除这些差距。猜猜看，如果你消除了这些差距会怎样？你就能把注意力转向下一个差距、再下一个差距、再下一个差距。（01:16:28）如果你一直这样做，就会一直专注于下一个差距、下一个……它们会随着时间越来越小。我不知道这是否是个很好的比喻，但我当了15年商学院院长，是年度教授奖得主次数最多的人，而且主要教难度大的课程，比如EMBA之类的。他有一个简单的秘诀。他教大二课程，而大二课程恰好有13节两小时的讲座[01:17:10不可听清]或其他形式。他会定期调查学生对每节课的反馈，不论原因，不论其他因素，每年都会砍掉第13节课。（01:17:26）因为从某种意义上说，这是最大的差距——客户、学生期望的与实际获得的之间的差距。他会用其他东西替代它，尝试其他方法。有人会问：这样每年都能获奖教授奖？答案是肯定的，因为进步。即使你教了25年，每年都坚持这样做，课程就会越来越好、越来越好、越来越好、越来越好、越来越好。所以，进步并不会让纯粹主义者觉得了不起，但我来这里不是为了让纯粹主义者觉得了不起，而是为了帮助人们进步。

turns.en: This makes me think about your water metaphor too, of just water eventually finding a way through. [inaudible 01:18:26] iterating, [inaudible 01:18:27] things better.
turns.zh: 这让我也想到了你的水喻，水总会找到出路的。[01:18:26不可听清]不断迭代，把事情做得更好。

turns.zh: 是啊，我对战略的思考很多都是自然而然的。我试着去问，世界通常是如何运作的，而我们所做的事情是否与世界的运作方式相一致？

turns.zh: 好的，这次对话非常愉快，我们讨论了所有我希望能涵盖的内容。我认为我们将帮助许多人重新审视他们对战略的思考。罗杰，你有没有什么想留给听众的话，或者在结束前想说的话？我们已经讨论了很多，可能没有什么遗漏的了。

turns.speaker: Roger Martin
turns.en: Well, on strategy, there's one piece of advice I'd say. People often ask me about people who are natural strategists, or they say, I'm not naturally good at that, I'm more of an operational guy or gal. And what I tell them is, I have never met this mythical beast called a great natural strategist. And they often throw back in my face, Lafley. They say, look, Lafley, he was known as a strategy genius. And I say, yeah, but when I interviewed him in depth about his background, for a paper I was writing, what I discovered was when he was in the Navy, as a whatever, I don't know, probably 25-year-old in the Navy, he had a job where he had to think about strategy, and was testing things out, and doing things, and the like. And then, I realized that he had been practicing strategy for decades before he became the CEO, decades. (01:20:04): And so, he just had more reps when he became CEO than almost anybody else that I've ever met. There's another guy, [inaudible 01:20:15], ex-CEO, now he's gone on to a higher level of Lego brand group, would be similar. So, great strategists that I have met have all one thing in common. They just practice. And anybody, there's no such thing as a person who is willing to practice strategy, who will end up saying, I'm operational, I don't do strategy well. Which links to our last thing about betterment. Just work on making different choices to solve problems. Not problems that I say, I'm not going to define your gap, it's one that you feel in your heart, I wish this were better. Work on it, if you do that, you'll be a great strategist. So, be encouraged, don't be discouraged. And the worst thing to do is to wait. People say, well, I've got all these operational concerns right now, and then I'll get to strategy later. You'll never amount to anything. Nobody who says that ever amounts to anything.
turns.zh: 嗯，关于战略，我想给出一条建议。人们经常问我，哪些人是天生的战略家，或者他们会说，"我在这方面不擅长，我更擅长运营工作。"我告诉他们，我从未见过所谓的天生战略家这种神话般的人物。他们往往反驳我，"拉夫利（Lafley）不就是个战略天才吗？"我会回应说，"是的，但当我为写一篇论文深入采访他时，发现他在海军服役时，大概25岁左右，就已经在思考战略、测试各种方案、执行任务了。"然后我意识到，在他成为首席执行官之前，他已经练习了数十年的战略。（01:20:04）：所以，他成为首席执行官时的经验比我见过的任何人都丰富得多。还有一个人，[音频缺失 01:20:15]，前首席执行官，现在已晋升至乐高品牌集团的高层，情况类似。因此，我遇到的优秀战略家都有一个共同点——他们不断实践。任何愿意练习战略的人，不可能最终说自己不擅长运营。这与我们最后提到的自我提升有关。只要努力做出不同的选择来解决问题，而不是我所说的"我不去定义你的差距"，而是你内心深处觉得"我希望事情能更好"。努力去改进吧，这样你就会成为一名出色的战略家。别灰心，最糟糕的做法就是等待。人们会说，"我现在有太多运营方面的担忧，等以后再处理战略问题。"但这样的人永远一事无成。

turns.zh: 不客气。感谢你让我度过了一段愉快的时光。
